title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The run used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer, a preregistered paired design with N=400 tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task). Primary outcome: safe‑deploy boolean per episode. Results (artifact-backed): complete pairs = 400; baseline successes = 400/400; guarded successes = 400/400; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. No runtime repairs or rollbacks occurred (repair_applied = false across episodes). We interpret this null effect as a ceiling effect produced by the preregistered shared‑candidate design and the chosen generator+validator configuration rather than evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general. We add the required construct‑validity discussion (same validator used as guard and scorer), quantify how the ceiling outcome invalidates the prospective power rationale, and point readers to the archived execution and analysis artifacts for full provenance and per‑task metadata.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being applied to NetOps tasks that translate operator intent into device configurations and staged rollouts. Prior work shows promise for intent→configuration translation and for verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair workflows in infrastructure contexts, and surveys call for action‑aware, end‑to‑end benchmarks that exercise rollout, canary, blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. We designed and preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) a focused paired experiment to measure whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM agentic pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The experiment intentionally used shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task) to isolate runtime guard acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates. Our contribution is an artifact‑backed, preregistered, paired evaluation and an evidence‑grounded analysis of why the chosen design produced a null result and how benchmark hardening could expose guard benefits.
sections.related_work: Intent→configuration translation and LLM‑assisted configuration generation have been documented in recent prototypes and papers (intent‑based NetOps, PreConfig, GraphSynth). Verifier‑augmented workflows (e.g., verifier‑guided IaC approaches) have shown improvements in related infrastructure domains. Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools can detect configuration errors offline; agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestration) are applied to AIOps/NetOps but introduce failure modes (hallucination, unsafe tool use) that motivate runtime guardrails. Reviews identify a shortage of action‑aware benchmarks that measure staged rollout safety and auditability; our experiment operationalizes a compact staging benchmark to probe these issues under a strict preregistered design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The preregistered plan specified a paired binary design with exactly N=400 deterministic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and two conditions per task: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (verifier‑augmented). Execution used shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared across conditions) to test validator accept/block/repair behavior on identical generated candidates. Model and runtime: declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; model_calls_used = 400 (one shared initial generation per task). The runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), which deterministically validates candidate configurations against task constraints; adapter policies allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Deterministic checks and exclusions: three‑replay consistency checks were applied; no tasks were excluded. Analysis: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; preregistered test = permutation‑based paired test. The archived executor reported exact McNemar two‑sided test, permutation p, bootstrap CIs (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples), and effect sizes.
sections.results:
Execution and reconciliation: start 2026-08-29; completion 2026-08-29; planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; model_calls_used = 400; no failed episodes; complete_pairs = 400. Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑backed): baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency: n_11 = 400; n_10 = 0; n_01 = 0; n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; permutation p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI for paired difference = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000); Cohen's h = 0.0. Repair_applied = false for all episodes; therefore median time‑to‑rollback is not computable (NA). Representative shared candidate example (artifact): pair-000001 shared candidate = "interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up" (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt). All per‑episode validator traces, raw responses, and provenance are archived in the execution and analysis artifact bundle.
sections.discussion: Construct validity and bias: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both the runtime guard (in the guarded adapter) and the post‑hoc scorer used to determine safe‑deploy outcomes for both conditions (validator_id/value present in execution/scoring/* artifacts). This conflation creates a construct validity risk: when the runtime guard and the scorer share validation logic and constraints, concordant outcomes are more likely and the comparison measures the validator’s accept/block behavior on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics. We explicitly disclose this bias and interpret results accordingly. Ceiling effect and power implications: the preregistered power rationale targeted detection of ~10 percentage‑point absolute change at N=400 under nontrivial baseline failure rates. Observed baseline_success_rate = 1.0 (400/400) sets the paired‑difference ceiling at 0.0 and makes detecting a positive guarded advantage impossible in this run; hence the preregistered power assumptions are effectively violated by the realized data distribution. We therefore present the confirmatory inference (p = 1.0, CI = [0.0,0.0], Cohen's h = 0.0) as an artifact‑backed null outcome whose interpretation is: given the shared‑candidate design and the chosen generator+validator, the guard had no opportunity to alter deployments because every shared candidate already satisfied the validator. Implications for future benchmark and experiment design: demonstrating runtime verifier utility requires designs that produce nontrivial generator failures or allow independent per‑condition generation (or adversarial prompt injection/fault injection) so the guard can block or request repair. The archived artifacts include per‑task payloads and difficulty labels; readers and follow‑on researchers can use the artifact bundle to construct hardened designs that exercise blocking and repair paths.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline against an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator+validator configuration, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and both conditions achieved 100% safe‑deploy on N=400 pairs; the guarded condition produced no measurable improvement. This null result arises from a ceiling effect induced by experimental choices and does not imply that runtime verification is unnecessary in broader settings. We release the preregistration, execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis outputs to enable replication and to inform benchmark hardening that exposes guard blocking and repair behaviors.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory): This study was produced under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy boundary. The autonomous run used the declared model version gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (single shared initial candidate per task; independent_condition_generation = false). The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints (selected pre‑lock by the Research Director) limited the work to generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. The experimental framework and preregistration are archived as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 and were frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). Tools and capabilities permitted: hosted model API calls (OpenAI responses interface for gpt-5-mini), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for configuration scoring and guarding, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, and paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically scored candidates and acted as an acceptor/blocker under the preregistered adapter policy; the execution contract allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but no repairs were applied in any episode (artifact field repair_applied = false across episodes). The study used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) as a preregistered design choice; this explicitly reduces generation variance across conditions and therefore measures validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates. The preregistered analysis plan specified a permutation‑based paired test for the primary estimand; the archived confirmatory analysis reports exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (artifacts indicate test = exact_mcnemar_two_sided, p = 1.0; permutation p = 1.0; bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived with the execution manifest (execution/* and analysis/* in the artifact bundle). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the autonomy constraints of the master prompt; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred (permitted by the track) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as final empirical evidence unless reproduced in the post‑lock run.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: tasks were synthetic and, under the shared_initial_candidate design and chosen generator+validator, produced universally valid candidates so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this limits sensitivity to verify a runtime guard benefit.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer (see execution/scoring/* artifacts); this conflation biases the comparison toward concordant outcomes and limits inference to validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop dynamics.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance across conditions and hence limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production runtime uncertainties, telemetry noise, adversarial intent, or operator workflows; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open.

Reporting gap: the archived evidence bundle contains per‑task difficulty labels (the representative sample of six tasks shows 1× medium, 2× hard, 3× very_hard). A complete per‑task difficulty histogram is available in the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle, but aggregated counts by difficulty were not summarized in the original top‑level manuscript artifacts; this reporting omission is explicitly preserved here as an unresolved reporting limitation and we direct readers to execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the archive for the full per‑task labels.
